HAZARD_SITES are executable source .py files (src/rebar/...), not non-executable instruction artifacts, so the structural-artifact grep exception does not apply.
advisory.finding: The two 'adoption' tests assert on the TEXT of the production source under test (read_text of the .py file, then `assert "atomic_write" in text` and regexes over temp-name spellings) rather than on behavior. This is source-grepping: it breaks on a behavior-preserving refactor (renaming/aliasing the helper, `from ...fsutil import atomic_write as aw`, wrapping in functools.partial, or any other correct atomic-write mechanism) even though no observable behavior changed.
scenarios: A future refactor imports the helper under an alias or via a thin wrapper: the string 'atomic_write' vanishes from the file and the test reddens despite identical behavior.
A correct alternative atomic write using tempfile.mkstemp inline (not named atomic_write) would fail the adoption grep while being behaviorally correct.

A regression at any of those sites that used a shared temp spelled outside SHARED_TEMP_PATTERNS (e.g. an f-string temp, tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile with a fixed name, or `Path(str(target)+'_tmp')`) would pass the grep and no behavioral test would catch it.
